diagrams.name: anat-p166-lymph-nodes
diagrams.title: Lymphatic system of the head and neck

labels.answer: Carries messages to and from the CNS
Connects the brain to the peripheral nervous system
Controls voluntary muscles, transmits sensory information to CNS
CN VIII Vestibulocochlear (sensory) — hearing and balance
CN III Oculomotor (motor) — eye movement, pupil constriction
CN IX Glossopharyngeal (both) — taste (posterior 1/3 tongue), parotid secretion
CN V Trigeminal (both) — facial sensation, muscles of mastication
CN X Vagus (both) — soft palate, pharynx, larynx, autonomic organs
CN VII Facial (both) — facial expression, taste, saliva

diagrams.name: anat-p170-trigeminal
diagrams.title: Trigeminal nerve (CN V) divisions and branches

cloze.section: Veins of the head and neck
cloze.text: The {{c1::pterygoid venous plexus}} receives drainage from the PSA, IA, infraorbital, deep facial and other veins.

cloze.section: Veins of the head and neck
cloze.text: The pterygoid plexus can be punctured during a {{c1::PSA}} block, causing a {{c2::hematoma}} or enabling infection to spread to the {{c3::cavernous sinus}}.

cloze.section: Veins of the head and neck
cloze.text: The {{c1::internal jugular vein (IJV)}} drains the brain, face and neck and runs deep with the common carotid artery and vagus nerve inside the {{c2::carotid sheath}}.

cloze.section: Veins of the head and neck
cloze.text: The internal jugular vein runs inside the carotid sheath together with the {{c1::common carotid artery}} and the {{c2::vagus nerve}}.

cloze.section: Veins of the head and neck
cloze.text: The {{c1::external jugular vein (EJV)}} drains the scalp and superficial face, runs superficial to the {{c2::sternocleidomastoid}}, and is often {{c3::visible}} during exams or dehydration.

cloze.section: Veins of the head and neck
cloze.text: Venous drainage pathway: face/oral cavity → {{c1::facial vein}} (and other tributaries) → {{c2::IJV or EJV}} → {{c3::subclavian vein}} → {{c4::brachiocephalic vein}} → superior vena cava → heart.

cloze.section: Veins of the head and neck
cloze.text: In the venous drainage of the face, the brachiocephalic vein empties into the {{c1::superior vena cava}}, which returns blood to the heart.
cloze.extra: Did you know: in 2023 ex-NFL player Mike Williams died of sepsis after a dental infection from retained tooth roots — oral infections can spread via venous pathways like the facial vein or pterygoid plexus to the heart or brain.

cloze.section: Lymph nodes of the head and neck
cloze.text: The {{c1::submental}} lymph nodes lie {{c2::under the chin}} and drain the mandibular incisors, tip of the tongue, lower lip center and chin.

cloze.section: Lymph nodes of the head and neck
cloze.text: The submental lymph nodes drain the {{c1::mandibular incisors}}, the {{c2::tip of the tongue}}, the center of the lower lip and the chin.

cloze.section: Lymph nodes of the head and neck
cloze.text: The {{c1::submandibular}} lymph nodes lie under the mandible near the angle and drain all teeth except the mandibular incisors and maxillary 3rd molars, plus the cheeks, anterior tongue and upper/lower lips.

cloze.section: Lymph nodes of the head and neck
cloze.text: The submandibular lymph nodes drain all teeth EXCEPT the {{c1::mandibular incisors}} and the {{c2::maxillary 3rd molars}}.

cloze.section: Lymph nodes of the head and neck
cloze.text: The {{c1::tonsillar (jugulodigastric)}} lymph nodes lie behind the submandibular nodes near the tonsils and drain the palatine tonsils, soft palate and posterior tongue.

cloze.section: Lymph nodes of the head and neck
cloze.text: The tonsillar (jugulodigastric) nodes drain the {{c1::palatine tonsils}}, soft palate and posterior tongue, and are often enlarged in {{c2::tonsillitis}}.

cloze.section: Lymph nodes of the head and neck
cloze.text: The {{c1::parotid (superficial)}} lymph nodes lie over the parotid gland in front of the ear and drain the lateral face, scalp and parotid gland.
cloze.extra: They are often confused with the preauricular nodes.

cloze.section: Lymph nodes of the head and neck
cloze.text: The {{c1::preauricular}} lymph nodes lie just in front of the ear and drain the external ear and lateral eyelids.

cloze.section: Lymph nodes of the head and neck
cloze.text: The {{c1::posterior auricular}} lymph nodes lie behind the ear and drain the scalp behind the ear and the outer ear.

cloze.section: Lymph nodes of the head and neck
cloze.text: The {{c1::facial}} lymph nodes lie along the facial vein on the cheek and drain the mucosa of the cheeks and lips.

cloze.section: Lymph nodes of the head and neck
cloze.text: The {{c1::deep cervical}} lymph nodes (superior and inferior) lie along the {{c2::internal jugular vein}} under the SCM.

cloze.section: Lymph nodes of the head and neck
cloze.text: The deep cervical lymph nodes are the {{c1::final common drainage}} of all head and neck nodes; deep infections or cancers drain here.

cloze.section: Lymph nodes of the head and neck
cloze.text: The {{c1::superficial cervical}} lymph nodes lie over the SCM and drain the skin of the neck and lateral face; they are not tooth-related but may swell with skin infection.

cloze.section: Lymph nodes of the head and neck
cloze.text: The {{c1::posterior cervical}} lymph nodes lie along the back of the neck at the posterior SCM border and drain the scalp and back of the head.

cloze.section: Lymph nodes of the head and neck
cloze.text: The posterior cervical lymph nodes are important in {{c1::viral}} infections such as mono or rubella.

cloze.section: Lymph nodes of the head and neck
cloze.text: The {{c1::supraclavicular}} lymph nodes lie just above the clavicle and drain the {{c2::thoracic cavity}}; they are not usually involved in oral infection.
The lymphatic system drains {{c1::excess fluid}} from tissues and returns it to the {{c2::bloodstream}}.
Lymph is a clear fluid containing {{c1::white blood cells}} but no {{c2::red blood cells}}.
Lymph is filtered through {{c1::lymph nodes}}, which trap bacteria, viruses and cancer cells.
Infections in the oral cavity often cause lymph node {{c1::swelling}} that can be {{c2::palpated}} clinically.
Lymphatic vessels of oral tissues drain into specific lymph nodes, which is essential for tracking the spread of {{c1::infection or cancer}}.
cloze.extra: Fun fact: the body has about 600–700 lymph nodes, over 100 of them in the head and neck.

cloze.text: The {{c1::palatine tonsils}} are rounded masses of lymphatic tissue between the {{c2::anterior and posterior faucial pillars}} on each side.
The {{c1::lingual tonsil}} is lymphatic tissue on the {{c2::base of the tongue}}, posterior to the circumvallate papillae.
{{c1::Lingual thyroid}} (not to be confused with the lingual tonsil) is a mass of thyroid tissue on the tongue caused by migration of the thyroid gland.
The {{c1::pharyngeal tonsils}}, also called {{c2::adenoids}}, are located on the {{c3::nasopharynx}}, behind the nasal cavity.
Mandibular incisors drain first to the {{c1::submental}} lymph nodes, then to the submandibular or deep cervical nodes.
All other mandibular teeth and most maxillary teeth drain first to the {{c1::submandibular}} lymph nodes, then to the {{c2::deep cervical}} nodes.
{{c1::Maxillary third molars}} drain directly to the {{c2::superior deep cervical}} lymph nodes, bypassing the submandibular nodes.
All dental lymph drainage converges at the {{c1::deep cervical}} nodes, which empty into the {{c2::jugular trunk}} and then the {{c3::subclavian vein}}.
cloze.extra: Infections follow this path, so swelling or tenderness at a node helps localize the source.

cloze.text: The nervous system works through {{c1::neurons}}, specialized cells that send messages using electrical and chemical signals.
cloze.extra: It controls movement, sensation, reflexes, salivation and automatic functions like breathing and heart rate.

cloze.text: The CNS includes the {{c1::brain and spinal cord}}.
The {{c1::brainstem}} (e.g., medulla), part of the CNS, is critical for {{c2::swallowing and salivation}}.
The PNS includes all nerves outside the CNS, especially the {{c1::cranial nerves}} that control the face, jaw and oral cavity.
{{c1::Sensory (afferent)}} nerves carry signals {{c2::to}} the brain (e.g., toothache, tongue temperature).
{{c1::Motor (efferent)}} nerves carry commands {{c2::from}} the brain to muscles and glands (e.g., chewing, salivating).
{{c1::Mixed}} nerves contain both sensory and motor fibres — most cranial nerves in the face are this type.
The {{c1::somatic}} nervous system is voluntary, controls {{c2::skeletal muscles}} (chewing, smiling, talking) and transmits sensory information to the CNS.
The {{c1::autonomic}} nervous system is involuntary and controls {{c2::glands, smooth muscle and heart}}, including salivary flow and pupil size.
The {{c1::sympathetic}} ("fight or flight") system {{c2::reduces}} salivation and increases heart rate and pupil size.
The {{c1::parasympathetic}} ("rest and digest") system {{c2::stimulates}} salivation and digestion and slows the heart.
There are {{c1::12}} pairs of cranial nerves that emerge directly from the brain.
cloze.extra: They control sensory, motor or both functions of the head and neck.

cloze.text: The cranial nerves with the highest dental relevance are CN {{c1::V (trigeminal)}} and CN {{c2::VII (facial)}}.
Cranial nerves in order: I {{c1::olfactory}}, II {{c2::optic}}, III {{c3::oculomotor}}, IV {{c4::trochlear}}.
cloze.extra: Mnemonic: On Occasion Our Trusty Truck Acts Funny, Very Good Vehicle Any How. Type: Some Say Marry Money But My Brother Says Big Brains Matter More (S sensory, M motor, B both).

cloze.text: Cranial nerves in order: V {{c1::trigeminal}}, VI {{c2::abducens}}, VII {{c3::facial}}, VIII {{c4::vestibulocochlear}}.
cloze.extra: Mnemonic: On Occasion Our Trusty Truck Acts Funny, Very Good Vehicle Any How.

cloze.text: Cranial nerves in order: IX {{c1::glossopharyngeal}}, X {{c2::vagus}}, XI {{c3::accessory}}, XII {{c4::hypoglossal}}.
cloze.extra: Mnemonic: On Occasion Our Trusty Truck Acts Funny, Very Good Vehicle Any How.

cloze.text: CN I, the {{c1::olfactory}} nerve, is {{c2::sensory}} for {{c3::smell}}.
cloze.extra: Not directly dental, but tested for brain injury.

cloze.text: CN II, the {{c1::optic}} nerve, is {{c2::sensory}} for {{c3::vision}}.
cloze.extra: Pupillary reflex: CN II sees, CN III reacts.

cloze.text: In the pupillary reflex, CN {{c1::II}} sees and CN {{c2::III}} reacts.
CN III, the {{c1::oculomotor}} nerve, is {{c2::motor}} for eye movement and {{c3::pupil constriction}}.
cloze.extra: Not dental, but damage = dilated pupil.

cloze.text: CN IV, the {{c1::trochlear}} nerve, is {{c2::motor}} for eye movement via the {{c3::superior oblique}} muscle.
cloze.extra: Not dental.

cloze.text: CN V, the {{c1::trigeminal}} nerve, is {{c2::both}} sensory and motor: facial sensation and {{c3::muscles of mastication}}.
cloze.extra: Most important for dentistry.

cloze.text: Trigeminal division {{c1::V2}} supplies the maxilla; division {{c2::V3}} supplies the mandible.
CN VI, the {{c1::abducens}} nerve, is {{c2::motor}} for eye movement via the {{c3::lateral rectus}}.
cloze.extra: Not dental.

cloze.text: CN VII, the {{c1::facial}} nerve, is {{c2::both}}: facial expression, taste of the {{c3::anterior 2/3}} of the tongue, and saliva.
CN VII controls the muscles of {{c1::facial expression}} and supplies the {{c2::submandibular and sublingual}} glands.
CN VIII, the {{c1::vestibulocochlear}} nerve, is {{c2::sensory}} for {{c3::hearing and balance}}.
cloze.extra: Not dental, but dizziness or hearing changes may be noted in head exams.

cloze.text: CN IX, the {{c1::glossopharyngeal}} nerve, is {{c2::both}}: taste of the {{c3::posterior 1/3}} of the tongue and {{c4::parotid gland}} secretion.
cloze.extra: The book's cranial-nerve figure labels CN IX "facial expression, taste" — that is an error; facial expression is CN VII.

cloze.text: CN IX supplies the parotid gland via the {{c1::otic}} ganglion.
CN X, the {{c1::vagus}} nerve, is {{c2::both}}: muscles of the {{c3::soft palate, pharynx and larynx}}, and autonomic organs.
CN {{c1::X (vagus)}} is involved in the {{c2::gag reflex}}; palatal movement is seen during oral exams.
CN XI, the {{c1::accessory}} nerve, is {{c2::motor}}: turns the head and elevates the shoulders ({{c3::SCM and trapezius}}).
cloze.extra: May be palpated when checking neck movement.

cloze.text: CN XII, the {{c1::hypoglossal}} nerve, is {{c2::motor}} for {{c3::tongue movement}}.
CN XII is tested by asking the patient to {{c1::stick out the tongue}} — {{c2::deviation}} indicates nerve damage.
CN V, the trigeminal, is the {{c1::largest}} cranial nerve; it emerges from the {{c2::pons}} and splits into {{c3::three}} major divisions.
{{c1::Trigeminal neuralgia}} is a chronic condition causing sudden, severe, electric-shock-like facial pain along CN V, most often {{c2::V2 or V3}}.
V1, the {{c1::ophthalmic}} division, is {{c2::sensory}} and supplies the forehead, upper eyelid and {{c3::tip of the nose}}.
cloze.extra: Not dental.

cloze.text: V2, the {{c1::maxillary}} division, is {{c2::sensory}} and supplies the maxillary teeth, palate, nasal cavity, upper lip and sinus.
The V2 division is anesthetized by the {{c1::PSA, MSA, ASA, GP, NP and infraorbital}} nerve blocks.
V3, the {{c1::mandibular}} division, is {{c2::mixed}} and supplies the mandibular teeth, chin, lower lip, tongue (sensory) and {{c3::muscles of mastication}}.
The V3 division is anesthetized by the {{c1::IA, mental, incisive, lingual and buccal}} blocks.
The {{c1::posterior superior alveolar (PSA)}} nerve supplies the maxillary molars, buccal gingiva and sinus.
The PSA injection carries a risk of {{c1::hematoma}} due to the {{c2::pterygoid venous plexus}}.
The {{c1::middle superior alveolar (MSA)}} nerve supplies the {{c2::premolars}} and the {{c3::mesiobuccal root of the 1st molar}} (if present).
The MSA nerve is absent in about {{c1::50%}} of people; the {{c2::ASA or PSA}} may compensate.
The {{c1::anterior superior alveolar (ASA)}} nerve supplies the {{c2::canines, incisors}} and facial gingiva.
The ASA nerve enters bone via the {{c1::infraorbital canal}} and is blocked with the {{c2::ASA or IO}} injection.
The {{c1::infraorbital (IO)}} nerve supplies the lower eyelid, cheek and upper lip and gives off the {{c2::ASA and MSA}}.
cloze.extra: It is accessed in the infraorbital nerve block.

cloze.text: The {{c1::greater palatine (GP)}} nerve supplies the posterior hard palate and lingual (palatal) gingiva.
The greater palatine nerve exits the {{c1::greater palatine foramen}} near the {{c2::2nd molar}}; it is used in palatal injections.
The {{c1::nasopalatine (NP)}} nerve supplies the anterior hard palate behind the incisors.
The nasopalatine nerve exits the {{c1::incisive foramen}} behind the maxillary centrals; it is a {{c2::painful}} injection site.
The {{c1::inferior alveolar}} nerve innervates the pulp of mandibular teeth but NOT the surrounding gingiva — so several injections may be needed to numb both.
Buccal gingiva of mandibular molars is innervated by the {{c1::buccal}} nerve.
Facial gingiva of mandibular anterior teeth and premolars is innervated by the {{c1::mental}} nerve.
Mandibular lingual gingiva and the floor of the mouth are innervated by the {{c1::lingual}} nerve.
The {{c1::inferior alveolar}} nerve supplies all mandibular teeth, runs in the {{c2::mandibular canal}}, and is the target of the {{c3::IA block}}.
The {{c1::mental}} nerve supplies the chin, lower lip and buccal gingiva of anterior teeth.
The mental nerve exits at the {{c1::mental foramen}} near the {{c2::2nd premolar}}; it is used in the mental nerve block.
The {{c1::incisive}} nerve supplies the mandibular anterior teeth; it is the continuation of the IA within the canal and is {{c2::not externally accessible}}.
The {{c1::lingual}} nerve supplies the {{c2::anterior 2/3 of the tongue}} and lingual gingiva.
The lingual nerve is commonly anesthetized with the {{c1::IA block}}; it does not run in bone.
The {{c1::long buccal}} nerve supplies the buccal gingiva of molars; it crosses the {{c2::anterior ramus}} and often needs a separate injection.
The V3 motor branches supply the {{c1::masseter, temporalis and medial/lateral pterygoids}}, creating the chewing motion.
CN VII controls the muscles of {{c1::facial expression}}.
The {{c1::chorda tympani}}, a branch of CN VII, carries taste from the {{c2::anterior 2/3}} of the tongue.
Because chorda tympani fibres travel with the lingual nerve, an {{c1::inferior alveolar nerve block}} can cause temporary {{c2::dry mouth or taste disturbance}}.
CN VII has {{c1::5}} terminal branches that pass through the {{c2::parotid gland}} but do not innervate it (the parotid is innervated by CN {{c3::IX}}).
Facial nerve branches from top to bottom: {{c1::temporal}}, {{c2::zygomatic}}, {{c3::buccal}}, marginal mandibular, cervical.
cloze.extra: Mnemonic: Tom's Zebra Bit My Cat.

cloze.text: Facial nerve branches from top to bottom: temporal, zygomatic, buccal, {{c1::marginal mandibular}}, {{c2::cervical}}.
cloze.extra: Mnemonic: Tom's Zebra Bit My Cat.

cloze.text: The {{c1::temporal}} branch of CN VII supplies the forehead and upper eyelid (e.g., frontalis, orbicularis oculi).
The {{c1::zygomatic}} branch of CN VII supplies the lower eyelid and upper cheek muscles.
The {{c1::buccal}} branch of CN VII supplies the muscles of the cheek and upper lip (e.g., buccinator, orbicularis oris).
The {{c1::marginal mandibular}} branch of CN VII supplies the muscles of the lower lip and chin.
The {{c1::cervical}} branch of CN VII supplies the {{c2::platysma}}.
Facial paralysis of CN VII is called {{c1::Bell's palsy}}; it may follow a virus, dental procedures or spread of infection.
Bell's palsy signs: sudden {{c1::one-sided}} facial droop, inability to {{c2::close one eye}}, loss of facial expression, dry mouth or altered taste.
In Bell's palsy, {{c1::protect the eye}} with artificial tears or by taping the eyelid shut at night if blinking is impaired.
Most Bell's palsy patients {{c1::recover fully}} within weeks to months; {{c2::corticosteroids}} (e.g., prednisone) or antivirals may be prescribed.

CN {{c1::V (trigeminal)}} provides sensation to the teeth, gingiva, bone and oral mucosa and supplies the muscles of mastication; CN {{c2::VII (facial)}} controls facial expression and does not innervate the teeth.
Anterior 2/3 of the tongue: taste = CN {{c1::VII (facial)}}; general sensation = CN {{c2::V (trigeminal)}}.
Posterior 1/3 of the tongue: taste and general sensation = CN {{c1::IX (glossopharyngeal)}}.
Base of the tongue: taste and general sensation = CN {{c1::X (vagus)}}.
Tongue movement is supplied by CN {{c1::XII (hypoglossal)}}.
In dentistry we focus on {{c1::exocrine}} glands, which have {{c2::ducts}} that release saliva into the oral cavity.
{{c1::Serous}} secretion is watery and enzyme-rich, containing {{c2::amylase}} to break down starch.
{{c1::Mucous}} secretion is thick and sticky and lubricates the oral cavity.
A {{c1::mixed}} gland contains both serous and mucous secretion; texture varies with the gland.
Functions of saliva: lubrication, digestion, {{c1::pH buffering}}, {{c2::antimicrobial defense}}, cleansing and {{c3::remineralization}}.
Salivary flow is controlled by the {{c1::autonomic}} nervous system.
{{c1::Parasympathetic}} stimulation gives more watery saliva; {{c2::sympathetic}} stimulation gives less, more mucous saliva (fight-or-flight dry mouth).
The {{c1::3}} paired major salivary glands are the {{c2::parotid, submandibular and sublingual}}; they produce most of the saliva.
{{c1::Minor}} salivary glands are hundreds of small glands scattered in oral tissues (lips, cheeks, palate) that keep mucosa moist.
Share of saliva: submandibular about {{c1::75%}} (book table: ~65% of resting), parotid about {{c2::20%}} (table: ~25%), sublingual about {{c3::5%}}.
cloze.extra: The book's figure and table give slightly different numbers; either way submandibular > parotid > sublingual.

cloze.text: The {{c1::parotid}} gland lies in front of the ear over the {{c2::masseter}} and secretes {{c3::serous}} (watery) saliva.
The parotid drains via {{c1::Stensen's}} duct and is innervated by CN {{c2::IX (glossopharyngeal)}}.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: Parotid → Parrots Sing → Stensen's duct.

cloze.text: Stensen's duct opens near the {{c1::maxillary 1st molar}}.
The parotid is the {{c1::largest}} salivary gland but produces only about {{c2::25%}} of total saliva.
The {{c1::submandibular}} gland lies beneath the mandible in the posterior floor of the mouth and secretes {{c2::mixed (mostly serous)}} saliva.
The submandibular gland drains via {{c1::Wharton's}} duct and is innervated by CN {{c2::VII (facial – chorda tympani)}}.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: Submandibular → Main Flow.

cloze.text: The submandibular gland produces about {{c1::65%}} of resting saliva; its duct opens at the {{c2::sublingual caruncle}} under the tongue.
The {{c1::sublingual}} gland lies beneath the tongue in the anterior floor of the mouth and secretes {{c2::mixed (mostly mucous)}} saliva.
The sublingual gland drains via {{c1::Bartholin's and Rivinus'}} ducts and is innervated by CN {{c2::VII (facial – chorda tympani)}}.
The sublingual is the {{c1::smallest}} major salivary gland; its {{c2::multiple ducts}} open directly into the floor of the mouth.
The TMJ connects the {{c1::mandible}} to the {{c2::temporal bone}} of the skull.
cloze.extra: The book calls it a hinge joint; strictly it is a ginglymoarthrodial joint — hinge (rotation) plus gliding (translation).

cloze.text: The TMJ is a {{c1::freely movable}} joint.
The TMJ {{c1::articular disc}} (fibrocartilage pad) separates the joint into {{c2::upper (gliding)}} and {{c3::lower (hinging)}} compartments.
The TMJ is innervated by CN V, division {{c1::V3 (mandibular)}}.

Opening the mouth (depression) starts with {{c1::rotation}} of the condyle in the {{c2::lower}} joint space, then {{c3::translation}} as condyle and disc slide forward onto the {{c4::articular eminence}}.
Muscles for opening the mouth (depression): {{c1::suprahyoid muscles}} and {{c2::lateral pterygoid}}.
Closing the mouth (elevation): the condyle slides back into the fossa, then rotates; muscles = {{c1::masseter, temporalis and medial pterygoid}}.
{{c1::Protrusion}} (jaw forward): both condyles slide forward via {{c2::bilateral lateral pterygoid}} contraction.
{{c1::Retrusion}} (jaw back): the condyles slide backward; muscles = {{c2::posterior temporalis}} and {{c3::digastric}}.
{{c1::Lateral deviation}}: the {{c2::lateral pterygoid on one side}} contracts, pushing that condyle forward while the opposite condyle stays stable — the jaw shifts to the opposite side.
cloze.extra: The book wording ("pushing the opposite condyle forward") is muddled; the contracting lateral pterygoid moves its own condyle forward and the jaw deviates to the other side.
